sk1_01.title: The Weight of the First Move
sk1_01.content:
The gymnasium had never felt so large.

Riya stood at the entrance, clutching her chess set against her chest, staring at rows of boards stretching all the way to the far wall. Today was the State Under-12 Chess Championship — the biggest tournament of her life. She had practiced for three months. She had studied openings, solved puzzles, and stayed up past midnight watching grandmaster games. She had felt ready.

But standing here now, she didn't feel ready at all.

Something was pressing against the inside of her chest — not pain exactly, but a weight she had never noticed before. The gymnasium was full of sound: chairs scraping, clocks clicking, the low murmur of forty-eight of the best young chess players in the state settling into their seats. Everyone seemed calm. Everyone seemed certain.

Riya found her assigned board and sat down. The girl across from her was already arranging pieces with steady fingers, not looking up. To Riya's left, a boy was quietly mouthing an opening sequence to himself. The tournament director was reading out the rules on a speaker that crackled slightly.

Riya's hands felt cold.

She thought of her parents waiting outside in the corridor — her mother sitting very still, pressing her palms together the way she always did when she was hoping very hard. She thought of her coach who had driven three hours to bring her here. She thought of her little brother who had drawn a picture of her holding a trophy and stuck it to the refrigerator with a smiley-face magnet.

All that hope. All that belief. All pressing down on her now.

What if she lost in the first round? What if she forgot her openings? What if this was the moment she discovered that all her preparation had been for nothing?

In the Bhagavad Gita, there is a moment very like this one. Before the great battle of Kurukshetra begins, the blind king Dhritarashtra sits far from the battlefield, his heart heavy with dread. He calls his minister Sanjaya to him and asks in a trembling voice: 'Sanjaya — the armies of my son Duryodhana and the Pandavas have gathered on that sacred field. Tell me — what is happening there? What are they doing?'

This question, which opens the entire Gita, is not really a military question. It is the question of someone who has a great deal at stake and has suddenly, terrifyingly, felt the weight of it all at once. Dhritarashtra loves his sons. He has watched a family rivalry build for years. Now it has come to this — two armies on a battlefield — and something in him is not ready for what might happen next.

His question — anxious, helpless, pressing — is the sound of inner pressure looking for a way out.

Riya recognised that sound now. It was the sound her own heart was making.

The tournament clock began. The director called: 'Round one — begin.'

Riya looked at the board. Sixty-four squares. Just those squares. She had been here before — not in this gymnasium, but in this moment. The moment before the first move, when everything is still possible and nothing is yet decided.

She breathed out slowly.

She had prepared honestly. She had worked hard. Whatever happened next would come from that preparation, and she would meet it one move at a time.

Riya reached forward and slid her first pawn two squares ahead.

The weight in her chest didn't disappear. But it shifted — from something that was pressing her down to something that was pushing her forward. That, she would later understand, is what inner pressure can become, when you are willing to make the first move anyway.
sk1_01.content_te:
జిమ్నాసియమ్ ఎప్పుడూ ఇంత పెద్దగా అనిపించలేదు.

రియా ద్వారం దగ్గర నిల్చుని, తన చదరంగపు పెట్టెను గుండెకు హత్తుకుని, గదిలో దూరంగా వరుసలుగా పరుచుకున్న చదరంగపు బల్లలను చూసింది. ఈ రోజు రాష్ట్ర స్థాయి పన్నెండు సంవత్సరాల లోపు చదరంగ పోటీ — ఆమె జీవితంలో అతి పెద్ద పోటీ. మూడు నెలలు శ్రద్ధగా సాధన చేసింది. ఓపెనింగులు నేర్చుకుంది, పజిల్సు సాధించింది, మధ్యరాత్రి వరకు నిపుణుల ఆటలు చూసింది. తాను సిద్ధంగా ఉన్నానని అనిపించింది.

కానీ ఇప్పుడు ఇక్కడ నిల్చుని చూస్తే, సిద్ధంగా ఉన్నట్లు అనిపించడం లేదు.

ఏదో ఒక భారం ఆమె గుండెలోపల నొక్కుతున్నది — నొప్పి కాదు, సరిగ్గా చెప్పాలంటే ఒక బాధ్యత, ఆమె ఇంతకు ముందు ఎన్నడూ అనుభవించని ఒక నిజమైన భారం. జిమ్నాసియమ్‌లో శబ్దాలు నిండి ఉన్నాయి — కుర్చీలు గీకే చప్పుడు, గడియారాల టిక్ టిక్, రాష్ట్రంలోని అత్యుత్తమ నలభై ఎనిమిది మంది యువ చదరంగ ఆటగాళ్ళు తమ స్థలాలకు చేరుకుంటున్న మెల్లటి గుసగుస. అందరూ ప్రశాంతంగా ఉన్నారు. అందరూ ఆత్మవిశ్వాసంగా కనిపించారు.

రియా తన నిర్ణయించబడిన బల్లను వెతికి కూర్చుంది. ఎదురుగా ఉన్న అమ్మాయి చూపులు ఎత్తకుండా నేర్పుగా పావులు సర్దుతోంది. పక్కన ఉన్న అబ్బాయి నిశ్శబ్దంగా ఒక ఓపెనింగ్ క్రమాన్ని పెదవులు కదుపుతూ అభ్యాసం చేస్తున్నాడు. పోటీ నిర్వాహకుడు చిన్నగా గుర్రుమనే స్పీకర్‌లో నిబంధనలు చదువుతున్నాడు.

రియా చేతులు చల్లగా అనిపించాయి.

ఆమె మనసులో బయట కారిడార్‌లో నిరీక్షిస్తున్న తల్లిదండ్రులు గుర్తుకు వచ్చారు — అమ్మ చాలా ఆశతో అరచేతులు నొక్కుకుంటూ నిశ్శబ్దంగా కూర్చుని ఉంటుంది. మూడు గంటలు నడిపించి తీసుకువచ్చిన కోచ్ గుర్తుకు వచ్చాడు. ట్రోఫీ పట్టుకుని నవ్వుతున్న ఆమె బొమ్మ వేసి ఫ్రిజ్ మీద అంటించిన చిన్న తమ్ముడు గుర్తుకు వచ్చాడు.

ఆ ఆశలన్నీ. ఆ నమ్మకమంతా. ఇప్పుడు ఆమె మీద భారంగా నొక్కుతున్నాయి.

ఒకవేళ మొదటి రౌండ్‌లోనే ఓడిపోతే? ఒకవేళ ఓపెనింగులు మర్చిపోతే? ఒకవేళ తన సాధన అంతా వృథా అయిందని ఇప్పుడే తెలిసిపోతే?

భగవద్గీతలో సరిగ్గా ఇటువంటి క్షణం ఉంది. కురుక్షేత్ర యుద్ధం మొదలుకాకముందు, గుడ్డివాడైన మహారాజు ధృతరాష్ట్రుడు యుద్ధభూమికి దూరంగా కూర్చుని, భయంతో మనసు భారంగా అనిపించింది. తన మంత్రి సంజయుని పిలిచి వణుకుతున్న గొంతుతో అడిగాడు: 'సంజయా — నా కుమారుడు దుర్యోధనుని సైన్యమూ, పాండవుల సైన్యమూ ఆ పుణ్యక్షేత్రంలో సమావేశమయ్యారు. చెప్పు — అక్కడ ఏం జరుగుతోంది? వారేం చేస్తున్నారు?'

గీత మొత్తాన్ని తెరిచే ఈ ప్రశ్న, నిజానికి ఒక సైనిక ప్రశ్న కాదు. చాలా పందెం పెట్టుకున్న ఒక మనిషి, అకస్మాత్తుగా అన్నింటి భారాన్ని ఒకేసారి అనుభవించినప్పుడు వచ్చే ప్రశ్న. ధృతరాష్ట్రుడు తన కుమారులను ప్రేమిస్తాడు. సంవత్సరాల తరబడి కుటుంబ వైరం పెరగడం చూశాడు. ఇప్పుడు అది ఇంతగా వచ్చి, రెండు సైన్యాలు యుద్ధభూమిలో నిల్చున్నాయి — మనసులో తర్వాత ఏం జరుగుతుందో అని ఒక భాగం సిద్ధంగా లేదు.

ఆయన ప్రశ్న — ఆందోళన నిండిన, నిస్సహాయమైన ప్రశ్న — లోపలి ఒత్తిడి బయటికి పోవడానికి ఒక మార్గం వెతుక్కుంటున్న శబ్దం.

రియా ఇప్పుడు ఆ శబ్దాన్ని గుర్తించింది. అదే శబ్దం ఆమె గుండె చేస్తోంది.

పోటీ గడియారం మొదలైంది. నిర్వాహకుడు పిలిచాడు: 'మొదటి రౌండ్ — ప్రారంభించండి.'

రియా బల్లను చూసింది. అరవై నాలుగు చదరాలు. కేవలం ఆ చదరాలు. ఆమె ఇంతకుముందు ఇక్కడ ఉంది — ఈ జిమ్నాసియమ్‌లో కాదు, కానీ ఈ క్షణంలో. మొదటి నడక ముందు ఉన్న క్షణంలో, అన్నీ ఇంకా సాధ్యంగా ఉన్నప్పుడు, ఇంకా ఏమీ నిర్ణయం కాలేదప్పుడు.

ఆమె నిదానంగా శ్వాస వదిలింది. నిజాయితీగా సాధన చేసింది. కష్టపడింది. తర్వాత ఏం జరిగినా ఆ పరిశ్రమ నుండే వస్తుంది, ఒక్కో నడకగా ఎదుర్కుంటుంది.

రియా చేయి చాచి మొదటి పావును రెండు చదరాలు ముందుకు నెట్టింది.

గుండె మీది భారం తగ్గలేదు. కానీ అది మారింది — తనను నొక్కే భారం నుండి తనను ముందుకు నెట్టే శక్తిగా. అదే లోపలి ఒత్తిడి చేయగలిగేది, ఎప్పుడైనా మొదటి నడక వేయడానికి సిద్ధంగా ఉంటే.
sk1_01.moral: Big challenges bring pressure before they bring answers. That tightness in your chest is not a warning to retreat — it is a sign that something truly matters to you. The first move is always the hardest, and it is also the most important.
sk1_01.moral_te: పెద్ద సవాళ్ళు సమాధానాలకు ముందు ఒత్తిడి తీసుకొస్తాయి. గుండెలోని ఆ బిగుతు వెనక్కి వెళ్ళమని హెచ్చరిక కాదు — అది నీకు నిజంగా ముఖ్యమైన విషయానికి సంకేతం. మొదటి నడకే ఎప్పుడూ అతి కష్టమైనది, మరియు అది అతి ముఖ్యమైనది కూడా.
sk1_01.activity: Before your next big challenge, sit quietly for two minutes and notice any pressure you feel in your body. Write one sentence: 'This matters to me because...' Then take your first step.
sk1_01.activity_te: నీ తదుపరి పెద్ద సవాలుకు ముందు రెండు నిమిషాలు నిశ్శబ్దంగా కూర్చుని శరీరంలో అనిపించే ఒత్తిడిని గమనించు. ఒక వాక్యం రాయి: 'ఇది నాకు ముఖ్యం ఎందుకంటే...' తర్వాత మొదటి అడుగు వేయి.

sk1_02.title: Counting Strengths Before the Storm
sk1_02.content:
Vikram had a red notebook.

He had started it the day his team was selected for the State Inter-School Science Innovation Challenge, and by now — four weeks later — it was nearly full. Not with formulas or diagrams, but with lists.

On the first page, written in careful block letters, were the names of every other team that would be competing. Next to each name he had noted what he knew: which school, how many trophies, whether they had won last year. Beside St. Peter's Academy he had written: 'Robotics experts — very strong.' Beside Greenfield High: 'Won nationals two years ago.' Beside the team from his own city rival, DPS North, he had underlined and circled: 'Best hardware setup. Two patent holders in Class 8.'

His teammates thought the notebook was strategic preparation. It was — but it was also something else.

Every evening before bed, Vikram would open the notebook and read through his lists. Then he would flip to the second section, where he had written out his own team's strengths. Nandini was brilliant at data analysis. Ravi could build almost anything from spare parts in the equipment room. And Vikram himself — his specialty was presenting, making complex ideas feel simple and exciting. 'We have good people,' he would tell himself. 'We can do this.'

But then his eyes would drift back to the first section, and he would start worrying again.

In the Bhagavad Gita, there is a scene very much like Vikram's evening routine. Before the battle of Kurukshetra begins, the Kaurava prince Duryodhana walks up to his teacher Drona and begins listing warriors — on both sides. He names Bhima, Arjuna, Yuyudhana on the Pandava side. He names his own champions: Bhishma, Karna, Drona himself, Ashwatthama. He says confidently: 'Our army is limitless. Their army is limited. Look at how many great ones stand with us.'

It sounds like the speech of a leader who believes in himself. But scholars of the Gita have noticed something underneath: Duryodhana is actually anxious. He is naming the Pandavas' warriors — naming them carefully and thoroughly — because he cannot stop thinking about them. If he were truly confident, he would not need to catalogue his fears so precisely.

The red notebook was Vikram's own version of this.

The morning of the competition, something unexpected happened. Their hydrogen-powered model — three months of work — arrived with a cracked fuel cell casing. A jolt in the transport box. Nandini's face went white. Ravi immediately crouched down to inspect it, already calculating whether it could be repaired.

Vikram felt that familiar tightening in his chest. He reached for the notebook by reflex — then stopped.

He realised the notebook had never actually helped. All those lists, all that careful cataloguing of threats and strengths — it had never told him what to do when something went wrong in front of him right now.

What helped was Ravi's steady hands, Nandini's quick recalculation of alternate data, and Vikram's own voice, calm and clear, telling their team: 'We have forty minutes. Let's focus on what we can fix.'

They did not win first place. They won something else: the judges' note that read 'excellent real-time problem solving.'

On the bus home, Vikram closed the red notebook and held it in his lap without opening it. Leaders feel pressure too — that is the Gita's quiet message in Duryodhana's anxious listing. The difference is not in having no fear. It is in knowing, when the moment comes, that the list in your head is less useful than the people beside you.
sk1_02.content_te:
విక్రమ్ దగ్గర ఒక ఎర్రటి నోట్‌బుక్ ఉంది.

తన బృందం రాష్ట్ర అంతర్పాఠశాల శాస్త్ర ఆవిష్కరణ పోటీకి ఎంపికైన రోజు నుండి ఆ నోట్‌బుక్ మొదలుపెట్టాడు. నాలుగు వారాల తర్వాత అది దాదాపు నిండిపోయింది — సూత్రాలతో కాదు, పటాలతో కాదు, జాబితాలతో.

మొదటి పేజీలో పోటీ చేసే అన్ని బృందాల పేర్లు జాగ్రత్తగా బ్లాక్ అక్షరాలలో రాశాడు. ప్రతి పేరు పక్కన ఏమి తెలుసో అది రాశాడు: ఏ పాఠశాల, ఎన్ని ట్రోఫీలు, గత సంవత్సరం గెలిచారా. సెంట్ పీటర్స్ అకాడమీ పక్కన రాశాడు: 'రోబోటిక్స్ నిపుణులు — చాలా బలంగా ఉన్నారు.' గ్రీన్‌ఫీల్డ్ హైస్కూల్ పక్కన రాశాడు: 'రెండు సంవత్సరాల ముందు జాతీయ స్థాయిలో గెలిచారు.' పట్టణంలోనే ఉన్న ప్రత్యర్థి పాఠశాల పక్కన అండర్‌లైన్ చేసి వృత్తం గీశాడు: 'అత్యుత్తమ పరికరాల సెటప్. ఎనిమిదవ తరగతిలో ఇద్దరు పేటెంట్ హోల్డర్లు.'

తన సహచరులు ఆ నోట్‌బుక్‌ని వ్యూహాత్మక సన్నాహంగా భావించారు. అది నిజమే — కానీ అంతకంటే వేరేది కూడా.

ప్రతి సాయంత్రం పడుకోముందు, విక్రమ్ నోట్‌బుక్ తెరిచి జాబితాలు చదువుతాడు. తర్వాత తన బృందం యొక్క బలాలు రాసిన రెండవ విభాగానికి తిప్పుతాడు. నందిని డేటా విశ్లేషణలో అద్భుతం. రవి పాఠశాల పరికరాల గదిలో అదనపు భాగాలతో దాదాపు ఏదైనా నిర్మించగలడు. విక్రమ్ స్వయంగా సమర్పణలో నిపుణుడు — క్లిష్టమైన ఆలోచనలను సులభంగా, ఆసక్తికరంగా అనిపింపజేయడం. 'మన దగ్గర మంచి వాళ్ళున్నారు' అని తనకు తాను చెప్పుకుంటాడు. కానీ అప్పుడు అతని కళ్ళు మళ్ళీ మొదటి విభాగానికి వెళ్ళేవి, మళ్ళీ ఆందోళన మొదలయ్యేది.

భగవద్గీతలో విక్రమ్ సాయంత్రపు అభ్యాసానికి చాలా పోలిన ఒక దృశ్యం ఉంది. కురుక్షేత్ర యుద్ధం మొదలుకాకముందు, కౌరవ యువరాజు దుర్యోధనుడు తన గురువు ద్రోణాచార్యుని దగ్గరకు వెళ్ళి రెండు వైపుల వీరులను లెక్కించడం మొదలుపెడతాడు. భీముడు, అర్జునుడు, యుయుధానుడు అని పాండవ పక్షంలో ఉన్నవారిని పేర్కొంటాడు. తన వైపు మహావీరులను కూడా పేర్కొంటాడు: భీష్ముడు, కర్ణుడు, ద్రోణుడే, అశ్వత్థామ. 'మన సైన్యం అపరిమితం. వారి సైన్యం పరిమితం. మా వైపు ఎంత మంది గొప్పవారున్నారో చూడండి' అని ధైర్యంగా చెప్తాడు.

ఇది ఆత్మవిశ్వాసం గల నాయకుని ప్రసంగంలా వినిపిస్తుంది. కానీ దాని వెనక ఏదో ఉంది: దుర్యోధనుడు నిజానికి ఆందోళనగా ఉన్నాడు. పాండవ యోధులను ఇంత జాగ్రత్తగా, ఖచ్చితంగా పేర్కొంటున్నాడు ఎందుకంటే వారి గురించి ఆలోచించడం ఆపలేకపోతున్నాడు. నిజంగా నమ్మకంగా ఉంటే, తన భయాలను ఇంత పూర్తిగా జాబితా చేయాల్సిన అవసరం ఉండదు.

ఆ ఎర్రటి నోట్‌బుక్ విక్రమ్ యొక్క స్వంత వేర్షన్.

పోటీ ఉదయం, ఊహించని విషయం జరిగింది. మూడు నెలల పని — జలజన్య శక్తితో నడిచే నమూనా — రవాణా పెట్టెలో కుదుపుతో ఇంధన కణ కేసింగ్ పగిలిపోయింది. నందిని ముఖం తెల్లగా పోయింది. రవి వెంటనే వంగి పరిశీలించాడు, సరిచేయవచ్చా అని లెక్కిస్తూ.

విక్రమ్ గుండెలో ఆ సుపరిచిత బిగుతు అనిపించింది. నోట్‌బుక్ తెరవాలని చేయి వెళ్ళింది — అప్పుడు ఆగాడు.

నోట్‌బుక్ ఎప్పుడూ నిజంగా సహాయం చేయలేదని అర్థమైంది. అన్ని జాబితాలూ — ఇప్పుడు తన ముందు తప్పు జరిగినప్పుడు ఏమి చేయాలో ఎన్నడూ చెప్పలేదు.

సహాయం చేసింది రవి స్థిరమైన చేతులు, నందిని వేగవంతమైన ప్రత్యామ్నాయ లెక్కలు, మరియు విక్రమ్ స్వంత గొంతు — ప్రశాంతంగా, స్పష్టంగా, బృందానికి చెప్పింది: 'మనకు నలభై నిమిషాలు ఉన్నాయి. సరిచేయగలిగేదానిపై దృష్టి పెట్టుదాం.'

వారు మొదటి స్థానం సాధించలేదు. వేరే ఏదైనా సాధించారు: న్యాయాధికారుల గమనిక — 'అద్భుతమైన తక్షణ సమస్య పరిష్కారం.'

యింటికి బస్సులో, విక్రమ్ ఎర్రటి నోట్‌బుక్ తెరవకుండా తొడమీద పెట్టుకుని నిల్చున్నాడు. నాయకులకు కూడా ఒత్తిడి కలుగుతుంది — దుర్యోధనుని ఆందోళనాగ్రస్తమైన జాబితాలో గీత యొక్క నిశ్శబ్ద సందేశమది. తేడా ఏమిటంటే భయం అస్సలు లేకపోవడం కాదు. క్షణం వచ్చినప్పుడు, మనసులో ఉన్న జాబితా కంటే ప్రక్కన ఉన్న వ్యక్తులు ఎక్కువ ఉపయోగకరమని తెలుసుకోవడం.
sk1_02.moral: Even leaders feel the pressure of what they face. The real test is not whether you feel anxious — it is whether you can turn from your list of worries to the people beside you.
sk1_02.moral_te: నాయకులకు కూడా ఎదుటి వారిపై ఒత్తిడి కలుగుతుంది. నిజమైన పరీక్ష ఏమిటంటే నువ్వు ఆందోళన పడతావా అనే కాదు — ఆందోళనల జాబితా నుండి నీ పక్కన ఉన్న వ్యక్తుల వైపు తిరగగలవా అనే.
sk1_02.activity: Make a list of three things that worry you about something coming up. Then write down one person who will be there with you. How can you shift your focus from the list to that person?
sk1_02.activity_te: రాబోయే ఏదో ఒక విషయం గురించి నిన్ను ఆందోళనకు గురిచేసే మూడు విషయాల జాబితా రాయి. తర్వాత నీతో అక్కడ ఉండే ఒక వ్యక్తిని రాయి. ఆ జాబితా బదులు ఆ వ్యక్తిపై నీ దృష్టిని ఎలా మళ్ళించగలవు?

sk1_03.title: When the Moment Becomes Bigger Than You
sk1_03.content:
Meera had been to the Republic Day ceremony every year since Class One.

She had stood in the school ground, shielding her eyes from the January sun, watching the flag rise each year with a familiar swelling in her chest — something between pride and something bigger than pride. She had never known what to call it.

But that was when she was in the crowd.

This year, Meera was the one holding the rope.

She stood at the foot of the flagpole in her pressed white uniform, the cord held lightly in both hands, her class lined up behind her in perfect rows. The school band was ready: fifteen students with brass instruments, a drummer who never missed a beat, and a girl with a piccolo who Meera had always privately thought was the best musician in the school. The principal stood at the microphone. The parents filled the benches. The younger children sat cross-legged on the ground, chattering and twisting to see everything at once.

Someone from the school office gave Meera a small nod: five minutes.

Meera had practised this. She knew exactly how many pulls the rope took to raise the flag to the top. She had practised four times in the week before, always at dawn before other students arrived. The flag rose smoothly every time. There was nothing technically difficult about it.

But standing here now, with five minutes left, the world felt very different from practice.

The band began its warm-up — just scales, just preparation — and even that small sound sent a vibration through Meera's chest. A koel was calling from the neem tree above the gate. The tannoy crackled as someone checked the microphone. One of the younger children dropped a water bottle and the cap clattered on the stone path. Every sound felt enormous. Every sound felt like it was heading toward something.

In the Bhagavad Gita, there is a moment when the war of Kurukshetra is about to begin and both armies are arrayed, trembling with readiness. Then Bhishma — the great elder of the Kaurava side — blows his conch. And then everything begins at once: the conchs of warriors on both sides fill the air, the drums begin, the earth and sky shake with the combined sound. It is not just noise. It is the announcement that something real, something vast and irreversible, is about to begin.

That sound — the sound that makes the very earth tremble — is the sound of a beginning that has grown bigger than any single person in it.

Meera felt that same vastness in her hands on the rope.

She thought: I practised four times and each time was just practice. This time is not practice. This time is the thing itself.

The principal finished speaking. The band director raised his baton.

The first note of the national anthem rang out, and with it came everything at once — the band, the crowd rising to their feet, the flutter of the breeze against the folded flag, the January light at exactly that angle that made the tricolour look brilliant even before it opened.

Meera pulled the rope.

Later, she would not be able to describe exactly what she felt as the flag unfurled above her — the orange and white and green catching the wind, the chakra spinning slightly as the cloth opened. She only knew that the moment was much, much larger than she was. That she was small in it, and that being small in it felt, somehow, exactly right.

Some moments are made to be bigger than any single person. That is not a frightening thing. That is what makes them worth being part of.
sk1_03.content_te:
మీరా ఒకటవ తరగతి నుండి ప్రతి సంవత్సరం గణతంత్ర దినోత్సవ వేడుకకు వెళ్ళింది.

ఆమె పాఠశాల మైదానంలో నిల్చుని, జనవరి సూర్యకాంతి నుండి కళ్ళు కాపాడుకుంటూ, ప్రతి సంవత్సరం జెండా ఎగురుతుంటే గుండెలో సుపరిచిత ఉద్వేగం అనిపించేది — అభిమానం మరియు అభిమానం కంటే పెద్దది మధ్య ఏదో. దాన్ని ఏమని పిలవాలో ఎప్పుడూ తెలియలేదు.

కానీ అది జనం మధ్య నిల్చుని ఉన్నప్పుడు.

ఈ సంవత్సరం, మీరా తాడు పట్టుకుని ఉంది.

ఆమె జెండా స్తంభం దగ్గర నిటారుగా నిల్చుని, ఇస్త్రీ చేసిన తెల్లటి యూనిఫాం వేసుకుని, రెండు చేతులతో తాడు తేలికగా పట్టుకుని ఉంది. ఆమె తరగతి వెనక వరుసలలో నిల్చుంది. పాఠశాల బ్యాండ్ సిద్ధంగా ఉంది — పదిహేను మంది విద్యార్థులు ఇత్తడి వాయిద్యాలతో, ఒక్క తప్పు లేకుండా మృదంగం వాయించే అబ్బాయి, పిక్కోలో వాయించే అమ్మాయి. ప్రిన్సిపాల్ మైక్రోఫోన్ దగ్గర నిల్చున్నారు. తల్లిదండ్రులు బెంచీలలో కూర్చున్నారు. చిన్న పిల్లలు నేల మీద కూర్చుని అటూ ఇటూ తిరిగి అన్నీ చూస్తున్నారు.

పాఠశాల కార్యాలయం నుండి ఒక వ్యక్తి మీరాకు చిన్న సంకేతం ఇచ్చాడు: ఐదు నిమిషాలు.

మీరా ఇది సాధన చేసింది. జెండాను శిఖరానికి ఎత్తడానికి తాడు ఎన్ని లాగులు పడుతుందో ఖచ్చితంగా తెలుసు. వేరే విద్యార్థులు వచ్చే ముందు తెల్లవారు ఝామున నాలుగు సార్లు సాధన చేసింది. ప్రతిసారీ జెండా సులువుగా ఎగురుతుంది. సాంకేతికంగా కష్టమైనది ఏమీ లేదు.

కానీ ఇప్పుడు ఇక్కడ ఐదు నిమిషాలు ఉంటే, ప్రపంచం సాధన కంటే పూర్తిగా వేరేగా అనిపిస్తోంది.

బ్యాండ్ వెచ్చుకోవడం మొదలుపెట్టింది — కేవలం స్కేల్సు, కేవలం సన్నాహం — మరియు ఆ చిన్న శబ్దం కూడా మీరా గుండెలో ఒక కదలిక పంపింది. పక్కన నేరేడు చెట్టు నుండి ఒక కోయిల పాడుతోంది. మైక్రోఫోన్ తనిఖీ సందర్భంగా స్పీకర్ ఒకసారి చటుక్కుమంది. ఒక చిన్న పిల్లవాడు నీళ్ళ సీసా వదిలాడు, మూత రాతి దారిమీద గలగలలాడింది. ప్రతి శబ్దమూ భారీగా అనిపించింది. ప్రతి శబ్దమూ ఏదో పెద్దది వైపు కదులుతున్నట్లు అనిపించింది.

భగవద్గీతలో కురుక్షేత్ర యుద్ధం మొదలుకాబోయే ముందు ఒక క్షణం ఉంది — రెండు సైన్యాలూ సిద్ధంగా, ఉద్వేగంగా. అప్పుడు మహావీరుడు భీష్ముడు తన శంఖం ఊదుతాడు. తర్వాత అన్నీ ఒకేసారి మొదలవుతాయి: రెండు వైపుల యోధుల శంఖాలు గాలిని నింపుతాయి, మృదంగాలు మొదలవుతాయి, భూమి మరియు ఆకాశం కలిసిన శబ్దంతో మేల్కొంటాయి. ఇది కేవలం అలజడి మాత్రమే కాదు. ఏదో నిజమైనది, విశాలమైనది, తిరిగి మళ్ళించలేనిది మొదలవుతోందని ప్రకటన.

ఆ శబ్దం — ఆకాశాన్ని నింపే, హృదయాన్ని మేల్కొల్పే శబ్దం — ఒక్కో వ్యక్తికంటే పెద్దగా పెరిగిన ప్రారంభం యొక్క శబ్దం.

మీరా తాడు మీద అదే విశాలత అనిపించింది.

ఆమె ఆలోచించింది: నాలుగు సార్లు సాధన చేశాను, ప్రతిసారీ అది కేవలం సాధన. ఇప్పుడు సాధన కాదు. ఇది స్వయంగా ఆ విషయమే.

ప్రిన్సిపాల్ ప్రసంగం ముగించారు. బ్యాండ్ డైరెక్టర్ తన కర్రను పైకి లేపాడు.

జాతీయ గీతం యొక్క మొదటి నోట్ మోగింది, మరియు దానితో పాటు అన్నీ ఒకేసారి — బ్యాండ్, నిల్చున్న జనం, మడతపడిన జెండాకు వ్యతిరేకంగా గాలి, జెండా తెరుచుకునే ముందే అన్నింటినీ అద్భుతంగా కనిపింపజేసిన జనవరి కాంతి.

మీరా తాడు లాగింది.

తర్వాత, జెండా తన మీద తెరుచుకుంటుండగా — నారింజ, తెలుపు మరియు ఆకుపచ్చ గాలిలో పట్టుకుని, చక్రం కొద్దిగా తిరుగుతూ — ఆమె అనుభవించింది ఏమిటో సరిగ్గా వర్ణించలేకపోయింది. ఆ క్షణం తన కంటే చాలా పెద్దది అని మాత్రం తెలిసింది. అందులో చిన్నగా అనిపించింది, మరియు అందులో చిన్నగా అనిపించడం, ఏదో విధంగా, సరిగ్గా సరైనదిలా అనిపించింది.

కొన్ని క్షణాలు ఒక్కో వ్యక్తికంటే పెద్దవిగా ఉండేందుకు ఉంటాయి. అది భయంకరమైన విషయం కాదు. అది వాటిలో భాగం కావడం విలువైనదిగా చేసేది.
sk1_03.moral: Some moments are meant to be bigger than any one person. When the trumpets sound and the earth trembles, your job is not to be unafraid — it is to hold the rope and do your part anyway.

sk2_01.title: Rise After the Fall
sk2_01.content:
The chess board had been sitting on Thatha's side table for eleven days.

Arjun walked past it every morning on his way to the kitchen — white pieces on one side, black on the other, frozen in the middle of a game that would never finish. Thatha had been winning, barely. His knight had cornered Arjun's queen three moves ago, and they had both laughed about it over evening tea, Thatha's glasses sliding down his nose as he leaned forward to study the board.

That was the last game they ever played.

Thatha had gone to the hospital on a Tuesday and had not come home. The funeral had been quiet and full of jasmine. Arjun had stood beside his Amma through all of it, shaking hands with relatives he barely knew, accepting plates of food he could not eat. Everyone said the right things. No one mentioned the chess board.

But Arjun saw it every day, and every day it made something heavy settle in his chest — not just sadness, but a kind of paralysis. What was the point of school, of cricket practice, of anything, when the person who taught him to castle and to never give up a pawn without a reason was gone?

He stopped going to chess club. He stopped reading the chess books Thatha had given him for his ninth birthday. He told his friends he was fine when he was not fine at all.

One Saturday morning, Amma found him sitting on the floor of Thatha's room, staring at the unfinished game. She did not tell him to get up. She sat down beside him and was quiet for a long time.

"He would have wanted you to move the queen," she said finally.

"I can't," Arjun said. His voice came out rough. "If I finish the game, it's like saying it's really over."

Amma nodded. "It is really over, beta. That part is true. But staying frozen in the middle of the game — that is a different kind of over. That is giving up while you are still alive."

That afternoon, Arjun opened the Bhagavad Gita reader his school had sent home for the term. He had been avoiding it. But he found the passage his teacher had marked for Chapter 2 — the moment when Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, and Arjuna's grief has made him unable to act.

Krishna's words were firm, not cruel: How has this weakness come upon you at this critical hour? This is not befitting a noble person. Do not yield to unworthy grief. The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead. Arise. Stand up. Do your duty.

Arjun — the boy, not the warrior — read those lines three times.

He understood something Thatha might have told him if he were still here: grief is real and it deserves its time. But staying fallen inside yourself forever is not grief — it is surrender. Courage does not mean you stop hurting. It means you rise even while the hurt is still there.

That evening, Arjun sat at the side table. He studied the board the way Thatha had taught him — not rushing, seeing three moves ahead. He moved his queen. Thatha's knight took it, just as it would have. Arjun moved his bishop into position. Checkmate in two moves, for the side that was not playing anymore.

He whispered, "You win, Thatha."

Then he reset the board, placed the pieces in starting position, and played a full game against himself — slowly, carefully, the way Thatha liked. He lost. He set the pieces up again.

Grief had not left. But something else had arrived alongside it: the willingness to move.

sk2_02.title: Two Voices, One Choice
sk2_02.content:
The group project was due on Friday, and Neha's notebook had become a battlefield of its own.

On the left page she had written, in blue ink: "Tell the truth. Priya copied three paragraphs from Wikipedia. It is not fair to the rest of us who worked honestly." On the right page, in pencil so soft it was almost invisible: "Priya is your friend. She has been having trouble at home. If you report her, she might fail the whole term. Is that what a friend does?"

Neha stared at both columns until the words blurred.

The project was a history presentation on the Mauryan Empire — twenty slides, a spoken script, and a bibliography that had to be properly sourced. Neha, Rohan, and Priya had divided the work three weeks ago. Neha had done the research on Ashoka's edicts. Rohan had built the slide design. Priya was responsible for the opening section on Chandragupta.

Yesterday, when Neha opened their shared document to combine sections, she recognised three paragraphs in Priya's part word-for-word from a website she had used herself during research. Priya had not rewritten them. She had not cited them. She had pasted and changed the font colour, as if that made it invisible.

Neha's stomach tightened. She closed the laptop. Opened it. Closed it again.

At lunch, Priya sat across from her eating her paratha with unusual quietness. "Is everything okay with the project?" she asked, not quite meeting Neha's eyes.

"Fine," Neha said. It was not fine.

That evening, Neha's Appa found her at the dining table with both pages of the notebook open. He read them without speaking, then poured two glasses of water and sat down.

"Which voice is louder?" he asked.

"Both," Neha said miserably. "That's the problem."

Appa nodded. "In the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna faces something like this — not a group project, but the same feeling. He sees people he loves on the other side of the battlefield. He sees his duty as a warrior. Both feel true. Both feel impossible. He tells Krishna: I am confused about my duty. I am your disciple. Please instruct me clearly what I should do."

"What did Krishna say?"

"First, he did not mock the confusion. Arjuna's conflict was real — love and duty genuinely pulling against each other. Krishna treated that seriously. But he also did not let Arjuna stay frozen forever in the middle. He asked him to look clearly at both sides, speak honestly about what he saw, and then choose with wisdom rather than panic."

Neha was quiet for a long moment.

"I don't want to destroy Priya," she said.

"And you don't want to betray your own honesty," Appa said. "Those are both good values. The question is not which one wins. The question is: what action honours both as much as possible?"

The next morning, Neha asked Priya to meet her in the library before school. She did not accuse. She said: "I noticed some sections that look copied. I think we need to fix them together before we submit. Can we sit down today and rewrite them properly?"

Priya's face went red. Then she nodded, slowly. "I was overwhelmed," she whispered. "My parents have been fighting every night. I ran out of time."

"I know," Neha said. "That's why I didn't go straight to the teacher. But we still have to fix it."

They spent two hours rewriting. It was awkward and uncomfortable and, by the end, more honest than any easy silence would have been.

Emotional conflict had not vanished. But Neha had learned what Arjuna learned on the chariot: when two true things pull against each other, the answer is not to pretend one of them is false. The answer is to see clearly, speak honestly, and choose.

sk2_03.title: When Sorrow Runs Deep
sk2_03.content:
Ishaan had not touched his cricket bat in two weeks.

It leaned against his bedroom wall like a stranger — the same bat he had scored forty-two runs with in the district semifinal, the bat whose handle he had rewound with fresh grip tape the night before the match that changed everything. He could not look at it without feeling something crack open inside his chest.

The match had been winnable. Ishaan's school needed eight runs off the last over with two wickets in hand. He had been at the crease, calm, counting the bowler's rhythm the way Coach Meera had taught him. Then on the fourth ball, a sharp catch at mid-wicket. Out. The next batsman run out. Done.

The team had lost by three runs.

Ishaan had walked off the field without speaking to anyone. He had not cried in front of his teammates — he waited until he was in the bathroom at home with the tap running. But the sorrow did not stay in that bathroom. It followed him to breakfast, to class, to bed. It sat on his chest like a stone.

"I can't do it again," he told his Amma on the Tuesday after. "What's the point? I had one job — eight runs — and I failed. Every time I think about cricket I feel sick."

Amma called Coach Meera.

Coach Meera arrived on Thursday afternoon with mangoes from her garden and no cricket gear. She sat on the floor of Ishaan's room — not on the chair he offered — and peeled a mango in silence until the sweet smell filled the room.

"Tell me the worst part," she said.

Ishaan stared at the bat on the wall. "I let everyone down. The whole team practiced for months. And I — I couldn't even score eight runs. I'd rather never play again than feel this again."

Coach Meera was quiet. Then she said: "Do you know what Arjuna told Krishna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, when his sorrow was so deep he could not fight?"

Ishaan shook his head.

"He said: I cannot kill my own teachers and family, even for a kingdom. What pleasure would victory bring? What use is a kingdom if the people I love are destroyed? I do not want to fight. I would rather be killed unarmed than kill them."

"That's — really sad," Ishaan said.

"It is. And Krishna did not say: stop being dramatic. He did not tell Arjuna his feelings were silly. Arjuna's sorrow was real and deep and it came from love — love for his teachers, his family, his whole world. Krishna heard all of it."

Coach Meera handed him a slice of mango. "But Krishna also did not leave Arjuna in that sorrow forever. He began to teach — gently at first, then more firmly. He helped Arjuna see that his pain was honest, but his conclusion — that doing nothing was better than doing his duty — needed to be examined."

"So my feelings are okay but giving up isn't?"

"Your feelings are real. They deserve to be felt. But feelings are not always the full truth. You are not only the boy who got caught at mid-wicket. You are also the boy who scored forty-two runs to get your team there. You are also the boy who has courage enough to pick up the bat again — not because the sorrow has gone, but because cricket is still part of who you are."

Ishaan took the mango. It was very sweet.

The next Saturday, he did not go to the full team practice. He asked Coach Meera to meet him at the nets alone. He picked up the bat. His hands shook a little. He played anyway.

Deep sorrow had not been dismissed. It had been met — with honesty, with patience, and with a path forward.

sk2_04.title: The Soul and the Seasons
sk2_04.content:
Ananya started the journal because her science teacher, Ms. Pillai, assigned it — but by October it had become something she actually needed.

The assignment was simple: track one object in nature through four seasons. Most students chose a tree or a bird's nest. Ananya chose the neem tree in her grandmother's courtyard in Hyderabad, the one with bark rough enough to scrape her palms when she climbed it as a smaller child.

Summer entry, written in June: "The neem is loud with leaves. Crows argue in the branches every morning. I feel hot and happy and annoyed by my brother in equal amounts. Everything is bright."

Monsoon entry, August: "Rain hammers the leaves. The ground smells like wet earth and jasmine from Paati's garden. I feel cozy inside but restless — stuck indoors, missing my friends. Same tree, different mood."

Winter entry, January: "The neem looks stripped and honest. No pretending to be full. I feel quiet too. School exams are close. Some days I am confident. Some days I am sure I will fail everything."

Spring entry, March: "Tiny green shoots on branches that looked dead. I felt surprised by hope. Then I got into an argument with my best friend Meera and felt terrible again. Both things true on the same day."

When Ananya read all four entries aloud in class, Ms. Pillai nodded slowly. "Notice something? The tree changed. You changed. But it was always the same tree — and always you."

That evening, Ananya video-called Paati and showed her the journal. Paati adjusted her reading glasses and smiled. "Your Ms. Pillai is wise. Let me tell you what Krishna taught Arjuna about this."

Paati's voice grew gentle and steady. "Krishna said: never was there a time when you or I did not exist, nor will there be a time when we cease to be. The soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body — just as the body itself passes through seasons. Heat and cold, pleasure and pain — they come and go. They are like visitors at a door. The wise person does not let them disturb their inner steadiness."

Ananya flipped to a blank page. "So the soul is like — the tree underneath the seasons?"

"Something like that," Paati said. "The leaves fall. New leaves come. The tree looks completely different in winter and summer. But the neem is still the neem. Your feelings change — happy, sad, angry, hopeful — sometimes all in one day. That is natural. You are not broken because you feel opposites. You are human."

"But what stays the same?"

Paati thought for a moment. "Your capacity to grow. Your ability to learn. The love you carry for people — even when you are angry at them. The you that watches all the seasons pass."

Ananya drew a neem tree on the blank page with four panels — green, rain-grey, bare, budding. In the centre of the trunk she wrote one word: still here.

When she moved to a new city the following year and lost the courtyard and the tree and her old street, she brought the journal. On lonely evenings she opened it and remembered: everything outside changes. The soul that watches — that learns, that loves, that keeps going — travels through all of it.

sk2_05.title: What Cannot Be Destroyed
sk2_05.storyTitle: Rahul and the House That Moved
sk2_05.content:
Everything familiar disappeared in three weeks.

Rahul's family sold the yellow house on Tulip Lane — the one with the broken gate that squeaked, the guava tree he had climbed since he was five, the window seat where he read comics until Amma called him for dinner. Appa's company was transferring him to Pune. New flat, new school, new everything.

Rahul packed his room in silence. Each object he placed in a box felt like putting a piece of himself in storage. His cricket trophies. His bookshelf with the spine-cracked Harry Potters. The poster of the Mars rover he had taped above his desk and replaced three times because the corners kept peeling.

On the last night, he sat on the empty window seat and thought: if all of this goes, what is left of me?

The new flat in Pune was on the fourteenth floor. It had clean white walls and a view of other identical buildings. Rahul's new room was the right size but felt like a hotel — temporary, borrowed, not his. At the new school, he ate lunch alone for the first week. His old friends sent messages, but the messages made him miss home harder, so he stopped reading them.

His Chithappa — his uncle who lived in Pune — visited on a Sunday with filter coffee and a chess set.

"You look like someone who lost more than a house," Chithappa said, setting up the board on the small balcony table.

"I did," Rahul said. "I lost everything."

Chithappa moved a pawn. "Did you?"

"My room. My tree. My friends. My whole life."

"Those things changed. That is true. They hurt to lose — that is also true." Chithappa looked at him steadily. "But let me tell you what Krishna said to Arjuna when Arjuna was afraid that everything meaningful would be destroyed on the battlefield. Krishna said: there has never been a time when you did not exist, and there will never be a time when you cease to be. What is real in you — the Self — cannot be cut by weapons, burned by fire, soaked by water, or dried by wind. It is eternal, unchanging, ever-present."

Rahul frowned. "That sounds very — cosmic. I'm just a kid who moved schools."

Chithappa smiled. "Cosmic things come in small packages. Think practically. What did you bring with you that no moving truck carried?"

Rahul was quiet. "I still know how to climb a tree — even if there isn't one here yet. I still make people laugh when I want to. I still care about cricket and Mars and finishing a book even when the ending is sad."

"There," Chithappa said. "That caring, that curiosity, that Rahul-ness — the truck did not take it. The white walls did not erase it. New school cannot destroy it unless you decide it has."

They played chess until the sun went down. Rahul lost twice and won once.

The next week, he joined the school cricket trial. His hands were nervous. His batting was still his batting — a little rusty, but real. A boy named Dev watched him play and said, "You hit that ball like you mean it. Sit with us at lunch?"

The yellow house was gone. But the indestructible things — curiosity, courage, the ability to begin again — had made the journey too.

sk2_06.title: The Flame That Stayed
sk2_06.content:
Kavya was nine when Thatha died, old enough to understand the word "gone" and young enough to not fully believe it.

Thatha had been the person who walked her to the corner shop every Sunday for peppermints, who told her stories about Krishna and Arjuna on the chariot while she braided her Amma's old dupatta through his fingers, who lit a brass diya every evening in the small alcove near the front door where the smell of camphor and sandalwood lived permanently in the wood.

The funeral had been long and full of people speaking in low voices. Kavya wore a white kurta and held Amma's hand and did not cry until everyone left and the house went quiet. Then she cried until her throat hurt.

For weeks after, she avoided the alcove. The brass diya sat there untouched, a thin line of old wax frozen along the rim. Every time she passed it, her chest tightened. Thatha had lit it. Thatha was not here. Therefore the diya should not be lit. The logic felt airtight and unbearable.

Her Paati — Thatha's wife — noticed. One evening she found Kavya on the sofa with a book she was not reading.

"Come with me," Paati said.

She led Kavya to the alcove, picked up the brass diya, and polished it with her pallu until it gleamed. Then she looked at Kavya with eyes that were sad and clear at the same time.

"You are older now than when you first heard the story of the little lamp," Paati said. "You deserve the deeper version."

She lit the wick. The flame caught — small, orange, steady, alive.

"When Arjuna was broken with grief on the battlefield, Krishna did not only tell him to stand up. He taught him about the soul. He said: the soul is never born, and it never dies. It is not slain when the body is slain. The one who thinks the soul kills or is killed does not know the truth. The soul is eternal."

Kavya watched the flame. "Thatha's body died," she said quietly. "I saw the coffin."

"Yes," Paati said. "And that is real, and your grief is real, and I will never tell you to pretend otherwise. Bodies begin and end. Bodies get old and sick and stop. That is the way of all living things — the diya's wax, the wick, the holder. They wear out."

"So Thatha is just — gone?"

Paati shook her head. "The body is gone. The person you loved — his stories, his kindness, the way he made you feel safe, the love he gave you — where does love go when someone dies?"

Kavya thought about it. "It stays," she whispered. "It stays in me."

"And in me," Paati said, placing Kavya's palm over her own heart, then over Paati's. "And in every person he touched. The soul is like the flame — you can snuff the wick, but the light does not vanish from the universe. It joins what is already bright."

Kavya looked at the diya. "Will you teach me to light it?"

Paati nodded. "Every evening. The way he did. Not because he is sitting here — but because the love he lit in you is still burning."

That night, Kavya's hands shook a little as she held the match. The flame rose. She was still sad — grief did not disappear like switching off a light. But the fear that Thatha had been completely erased began to soften.

The body ends. The love — the soul's light — does not.

sk2_07.title: New Clothes, Same Self
sk2_07.micro_theme_te: కొత్త శరీరాలు, అదే ఆత్మ — దానికి హాని చేయలేరు
sk2_07.content:
Vikram's science fair project was about change — and it changed something in him too.

He had chosen a topic his teacher called "ambitious": demonstrating how matter transforms but never truly disappears. His display board had three sections. Section one: a piece of paper burned in a metal tray — ash left behind, but the matter had gone somewhere, into smoke and heat. Section two: an ice cube melted in a beaker — solid to liquid, same water, different form. Section three: his Appa's old cotton shirt cut into strips and rewoven on a small loom Paati had in her cupboard — new shape, same threads.

The morning of the fair, Vikram stood beside his board nervously adjusting the strips of rewoven cloth. A judge in a blue lanyard stopped and read his title: "Changing Forms, Continuing Essence."

"Explain this to me," the judge said.

Vikram took a breath. "Fire can burn paper, but the stuff the paper was made of doesn't vanish — it changes form. Water can melt ice, freeze it again, boil it into steam. The water is still water. And cloth — " he held up the rewoven strip, " — can be cut and woven into something new, but the cotton fibres are the same fibres."

The judge nodded. "And the Gita connection? Your teacher mentioned you had one."

Vikram had not expected this question in front of other students. He felt his ears go warm. But he had practiced with Appa, so he answered:

"In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna teaches Arjuna that the soul is like this. Weapons cannot cut it. Fire cannot burn it. Water cannot wet it. Wind cannot dry it. The judge looked genuinely interested. "And what does that mean for you — not cosmically, but practically?"

sk5_01.title: Arjun Asks Krishna
sk5_01.content: At the start of Chapter 5, Arjuna speaks like a student confused by two paths. Krishna had praised giving up selfish work, and also praised selfless action. Krishna explains that both paths can lead to the goal, but for most people, doing duty with a steady mind—karma yoga—is often the stronger road. Peace comes when action and wisdom walk together.
sk5_01.content_te: అధ్యాయం 5 ప్రారంభంలో అర్జునుడు రెండు మార్గాల మధ్య గందరగోళంలో ఉన్న విద్యార్థిలా మాట్లాడాడు. కృష్ణుడు స్వార్థ పని వదిలివేయడాన్ని, నిస్వార్థ చర్యను కూడా ప్రశంసించాడు. sk5_01.moral: You can be active and peaceful at the same time.
sk5_01.moral_te: మీరు ఒకే సమయంలో చురుకుగా మరియు ప్రశాంతంగా ఉండవచ్చు.

sk5_02.content: Krishna teaches in Chapter 5 that a sage sees honor and insult like passing clouds. The sun shines; clouds sometimes cover it, but the sun does not stop being the sun. A student named Kiran was mocked online for a spelling mistake, then praised the next day for helping a new classmate. Kiran noticed how quickly feelings changed. Remembering the Gita, Kiran decided not to ride the roller coaster of praise and blame. Doing the right thing became more important than looking perfect.

sk5_02.moral: Praise and blame both pass away—stay steady.
sk5_02.moral_te: ప్రశంస మరియు నింద రెండూ గడిచిపోతాయి—స్థిరంగా ఉండండి.

sk5_02.activity_te: మీరు ఇటీవల విన్న ఒక మంచి మాట, ఒక చెడు మాట రాయండి. మీ శీలానికి ఏది ముఖ్యమైనది?

sk5_03.title: Equal Vision
sk5_03.storyTitle: The Cow, the Dog, and the King
sk5_03.content: In later verses of Chapter 5, Krishna describes the wise person who sees the same reality in a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a wise scholar. This does not mean all beings look alike—it means the same divine spark lives in each. A student watched classmates laugh at a janitor, then bow to the principal. She felt uneasy. sk5_03.moral: Treat friends and strangers with the same kindness.

sd1_01.title: The Big Day
sd1_01.storyTitle: Gulu and the Great Forest Race
sd1_01.content:
Little Gulu the squirrel sat at the edge of the Giant Park. Warm morning light lay on the grass like a golden blanket. Today was the day of the Great Forest Race, and everything felt very, very big.

Gulu saw the fast deer stretching their legs and the strong bears warming up near the old banyan tree. Families chattered. Leaves rustled. His heart went thump-thump inside his chest, like a tiny drum only he could hear.

"Too small for this," whispered a worried voice in his head.

His friend Kaka the crow called from a low branch, "You came! Good. But don't just stare—run when the horn blows!"

Gulu's paws wanted to hide. Instead, he remembered what Grandmother Owl had told him last night, reading from the old Gita story: even blind King Dhritarashtra could not see the field, but he asked his friend Sanjaya, "What is happening on the Field of Truth?" The king did not rush. He wanted to understand the scene before the big day truly began.

"So watching is allowed?" Gulu had asked.

"Watching is wise," Grandmother Owl had answered.

Gulu stood on his tiptoes and looked carefully. He saw where the path turned muddy. He saw where the deer would leap. He saw where the bears took wide steps. He noticed a narrow line of dry moss along the fence—small, but perfect for quick paws.

At the starting line, animals crowded and pushed. Gulu did not push back. He breathed in... and out... and watched, just like Prince Duryodhana in the next part of the story, who looked at the whole army before saying a single word to his teacher.

The horn blew. Deer shot forward like arrows. Bears thundered. Gulu waited one heartbeat—not from fear, but from quiet courage. Then he ran along the moss path his eyes had found.

Halfway through, he stumbled on a root. Kaka cawed, "Get up!" Gulu paused, looked at the root, looked at the finish hill, and ran again. The butterflies in his tummy did not vanish—they changed. They felt less like heavy clouds and more like brave sparks lighting his way.

Gulu did not win first place. The deer did. But Gulu crossed the finish line with his chest lifted, paws muddy, eyes bright. The forest cheered not only for the fastest, but for the small squirrel who had watched first, chosen his path, and run with a joyful, determined heart.

Quiet courage, Gulu learned, is not the loudest roar. It is the steady choice to see clearly—and then take one brave step.
sd1_01.content_te:
చిన్న అడవి ఉడుత గులు పెద్ద పార్క్ అంచున కూర్చున్నాడు. ఉదయం వెచ్చని సూర్యకాంతి పచ్చ గడ్డి మీద బంగారు దుప్పటి లా పడి ఉంది. ఈ రోజు గొప్ప అడవి పరుగు — అన్నీ చాలా, చాలా పెద్దగా అనిపించాయి.

వేగమైన జింకలు కాళ్లు విస్తరించుకుంటున్నాయి. బలమైన ఎలుగుబంట్లు పాత మర్రి చెట్టు దగ్గర సాధన చేస్తున్నాయి. కుటుంబాలు మాట్లాడుకుంటున్నాయి. ఆకులు చపచప మఱిపిస్తున్నాయి. గులు గుండె thump-thump అని కొట్టుకుంది — అతనికే వినిపించే చిన్న డ్రమ్ లా.

"ఇది నాకు చాలా పెద్దది," అని మనస్సులో ఒక చింతిత గొంతు గుసగుసలాడింది.

అతని స్నేహితుడు కాకి కాకా తక్కువ కొమ్మ నుండి అన్నాడు, "వచ్చావ! బాగుంది. కానీ చూస్తూనే ఉండకు — బాక ఊదినప్పుడు పరుగెత్తు!"

గులు పాదాలు దాక్కుకోవాలని అనిపించాయి. కానీ రాత్రి అజ్జమ్మ గedu పitta గీతా కథ చెప్పింది గుర్తు వచ్చింది: అంధుడైన ధృతరాష్ట్ర రాజు మైదానం చూడలేకపోయినా, తన స్నేహితుడు సంజయను అడిగాడు — "ధర్మ క్షేత్రంలో ఏమి జరుగుతోంది?" రాజు తొందరపెట్టలేదు. పెద్ద రోజు నిజంగా మొదలవ్వడానికి ముందు పరిస్థితిని అర్థం చేసుకోవాలని అనుకున్నాడు.

"అంటే చూడడం సరైనదా?" గులు అడిగాడు.

"చూడడం తెలివైనది," అజ్జమ్మ గedu పitta అన్నది.

గులు అడుగుల మీద ఎత్తి జాగ్రత్తగా చూశాడు. ఎక్కడ మట్టి ముదురుగా ఉందో, జింకలు ఎక్కడ దూకుతారో, ఎలుగుబంట్లు ఎక్కడ విస్తృత అడుగులు వేస్తారో చూశాడు. కంచె పక్కన పొడి moss బాగా ఇరుకైన మార్గం — చిన్న పాదాలకు అద్భుతం.

స్టార్ట్ లైన్‌లో జంతువులు నెట్టుకుంటున్నారు. గులు తిరిగి నెట్టలేదు. శ్వాస తీసుకున్నాడు... వదిలాడు... చూశాడు — కథలోని తదుపరి భాగంలో రాకుమారుడు దుర్యోధనుడు గురువుకు ఒక్క మాట మాట్లాడకముందే మొత్తం సైన్యాన్ని చూశాడు.

బాక ఊదింది. జింకలు బాణాల లా ముందుకు దూసుకుపోయాయి. ఎలుగుబంట్లు గర్జించాయి. గులు ఒక గుండె కొట్టుకునే క్షణం వేచి ఉన్నాడు — భయం కాదు, నిశ్శబ్ద ధైర్యం. తర్వాత కళ్లు కనుగొన్న moss మార్గంలో పరిగెత్తాడు.

మధ్యలో ఒక వేరు మీద జారిపడాడు. కాకా "లే!" అని అరిచింది. గులు ఆగి, వేరు చూశాడు, ముగింపు కొండ చూశాడు, మళ్లీ పరిగెత్తాడు. కడుపulo సీతాకోక చిలukalu అగిపోle da — avi maaraayi. Bhari meghala la kaadu, dhairyamaina merupula laga anipinchaayi.

మొదటి sthanam raadu. Jinka gelichindi. Kaani Gulu finish line daati tana chati ettukoni, paadalu drushthi thota mud tho, kallu merisinavi. Adavi vegamaina vaarikosam kuda, mundu chusi, tana daari emchukoni, santoshamga mariyu drudha hrudayam tho parigettina chinna squirrel kosam kuda jai jai annaru.

Nishshabda dhairyam ante pedda garjan kaadu ani Gulu nerchukunnadu. Spashtamga chusi, taruvaata oka dhairyamaina adugu veyadam.
sd1_01.moral: Quiet courage begins when you watch carefully, understand the scene, and then take one brave step—even if your heart goes thump-thump.
sd1_01.moral_te: నిశ్శబ్ద ధైర్యం జాగ్రత్తగా చూడడం, పరిస్థితిని అర్థం చేసుకోవడం, తర్వాత ఒక ధైర్యమైన అడుగు వేయడం — గుండె thump-thump అయినా.

sd1_02.title: The Inner Brave
sd1_02.content:
The Great Forest Race had started, but Gulu the squirrel reached a place where the path split in two. One path was bright with morning sun. One path was shadowy and cool. Gulu gripped his lucky twig like a tiny bow. "Which way is the right way?" he wondered.

Above him, a small leaf flag with a monkey symbol fluttered in the breeze. It reminded Gulu of the brave stories of Hanuman. Gulu stood a little taller. His chest felt warm, like he was finding his inner brave.

Grandmother Owl landed softly on a low branch. "Don't just pick a side because you're in a hurry, Gulu," she hooted. "A true leader looks at everything first."

"Can we go to the very middle?" Gulu asked. He wanted to see the bright path and the shadowy path at the same time. He wanted to be a Middle-Seeker.

Grandmother Owl nodded. Together they walked to the center of the crossroad. The forest was noisy there. Some animals shouted, "Go left!" Others shouted, "Go right!" Gulu did not shout. He just stood still and listened.

Standing in the middle was like having a secret window. Gulu looked left and saw sharp thorns hiding in the grass. He looked right and saw a path that was very slippery after the rain. Both sides looked tricky.

Because he stayed in the middle, Gulu saw something no one else saw. Right between the two noisy paths was a secret trail of soft, green moss—gentle, safe, and perfect for small paws.

"Look!" Gulu called out. By standing his ground in the middle, he had found the safest way for everyone. The other animals stopped shouting and looked at Gulu with wide eyes.

Gulu did not just run ahead alone. He led. He picked up his twig-bow and stepped onto the moss. He wasn't afraid of the paths anymore because he had seen them both clearly.

"I found my Inner Brave," Gulu whispered. Grandmother Owl winked. Taking the lead wasn't about being first—it was about finding the truth for everyone.

Gulu remembered the Gita story Grandmother Owl had told him: brave Arjuna, with Hanuman on his flag, lifted his bow when the challenge began. Then he asked Krishna to stop the chariot in the middle of the field so he could see everyone clearly before choosing. That was the same kind of brave—standing in the middle to see the whole picture.

sd1_03.title: It's Okay to be Nervous
sd1_03.content:
Gulu was right in the middle of the forest path. But suddenly, his paws felt like they were made of jelly. The finish line felt a million miles away.

His thump-thump heart was so loud he thought the squirrels in the next tree could hear it. His mouth felt dry, like he had swallowed a puff of dust.

Gulu sat down on a soft patch of moss. He put his lucky twig-bow on the ground. "I don't feel like a hero today," he whispered.

Grandmother Owl swooped down. "What's wrong, little runner?" she asked. Gulu sniffled. "My butterflies are too big. They are heavy like rocks."

"Gulu," Grandmother Owl whispered, "did you know that even the Great Prince Arjuna sat down because he felt shaky? Being a hero doesn't mean you are never nervous."

Gulu looked surprised. "Really? A Prince with a golden bow felt shaky paws too?" Grandmother Owl nodded. "Yes. The bravest thing he did was say it out loud."

Gulu took a slow breath. In... and out. He realized that the butterflies weren't trying to stop him. They were just his Power Engines warming up.

"It's okay to feel nervous," Gulu told his butterflies. "You can stay. We can run together." The butterflies didn't vanish, but they felt lighter.

Gulu picked up his lucky twig. His paws still felt a little bit tingly, but they weren't jelly anymore. He stood up and looked at the finish hill.

Gulu didn't run like a lightning bolt. He ran like a steady little stream. He knew that heroes aren't people who have no fear—they are people who keep going even with shaky paws.

Grandmother Owl had told him the Gita story: when brave Arjuna saw everyone he loved ready on the field, his legs felt weak and his mouth went dry. He told Krishna honestly how he felt. Then he sat down in his chariot and put his bow aside—just long enough to breathe before being brave again.

sd2_01.title: Stand Up Again
sd2_01.content:
Meera had practiced her school dance for three whole weeks. She knew every step — tap, spin, bow. She counted beats in the shower and in the lunch line. On the day of the show, the hall was full. Parents sat in rows like a garden of bright shirts and eager faces. The stage lights were warm on her cheeks. Meera's heart beat fast, but she smiled. This was her moment.

Then, halfway through the spin, her foot slipped on a shiny patch of floor someone had polished too much. Down she went — knees first, then hands. The music kept playing for three more beats that felt like three hours. For one terrible second, the whole room seemed to hold its breath.

Meera's eyes filled with hot tears. She wanted to crawl behind the curtain and never come out. "I'm done," she whispered to the floor. "I'm the girl who fell."

After the show, her Amma knelt beside her in the hallway where the smell of jasmine garlands hung in the air. She did not say, "Don't cry." She said, "That fall hurt — your knees and your pride. Both matter."

Coach Priya joined them with a water bottle and a clean towel. "Even the best dancers fall," she said. "On the biggest stages in the world, people fall. Courage is not never falling. Courage is standing up again."

Meera remembered something Amma had read from the Gita at bedtime. When Arjuna felt weak with sorrow, Krishna did not tell him to stay on the ground forever. Krishna told him to rise — to stand up for what mattered, even when his heart felt heavy.

The next morning, Meera's knees were bruised purple, but she put on her dance shoes anyway. She went to the empty hall and stood in the middle of the stage where the shiny patch still gleamed. She took a breath. She did one slow spin. Then another. Her foot stayed steady.

"Again," she told herself quietly.

At practice that week, she fell once more — a small wobble, not a crash. This time she laughed, stood up, and bowed to her reflection in the mirror as if the whole audience were cheering not for a perfect girl, but for a brave one who got back up.

Falling had been part of her story. Standing up again was the part she chose.

sd2_02.title: The Wise First Words
sd2_02.micro_theme: Wise teaching meets a sad heart
sd2_02.content:
Rohan opened his report card on the kitchen table and felt his stomach drop like an elevator. Maths — a red mark he did not expect. Science — lower than last term. He had studied at the dining table every evening. He really had. But the numbers on the paper looked like a door closing in his face.

He ran to his room and buried his face in his pillow, which smelled like his laundry soap and disappointment. "I'm stupid," he muffled into the fabric. "I'll never be good enough."

His Chithi — his aunt — knocked softly and sat on the edge of his bed. She did not grab the report card right away. She waited until Rohan's shoulders stopped shaking, her hand resting on the blanket.

"Tell me the sad part," she said.

"I worked hard and still failed," Rohan whispered. "Everyone will think I'm dumb."

Chithi nodded. "That hurts. It is okay to feel sad today. Sadness is not the enemy. Staying stuck in it forever is the trap."

Then she opened a small book on her phone — a picture of Krishna and Arjuna on a chariot between two armies. "When Arjuna's heart was breaking on the battlefield, Krishna did not start with hard rules. His first teaching was gentle but firm. He said: the wise do not grieve for what cannot be changed. What has happened has happened. Crying forever will not turn yesterday's mark into today's A-plus."

Rohan peeked at her. "So I shouldn't care?"

"No, dear heart. Care very much. Care enough to learn. But do not drown in a sadness that keeps you from tomorrow's work. Grieve the mark — then rise."

They walked back to the kitchen together. Chithi made hot chocolate with extra foam. Rohan spread his books on the table. One maths problem at a time, they found where he had gone wrong — not because he was stupid, but because one tricky step about fractions had confused him every time.

By bedtime, Rohan still felt disappointed. The red mark was still real. But the heavy blanket of "never good enough" had lifted a little. He wrote on a sticky note and stuck it on his desk: Ask Chithi for maths help every Tuesday.

Sadness had visited. Wisdom had not asked him to pretend he was happy. It had asked him not to stay fallen inside his mind.

sd2_03.title: Seasons of Feelings
sd2_03.content:
In the middle of Ananya's courtyard stood an old neem tree with rough bark that scratched her palms when she climbed. She had grown up running around its trunk, tying friendship bracelets on a low branch, and sharing ice pops in its shade with the neighbor kids.

In summer, its shade was cool and green. In monsoon, rain drummed on the broad leaves like fingers on a table. In winter, the tree looked sleepy and bare, honest about resting. In spring, tiny new leaves appeared like green fireworks against the blue sky.

One year, Ananya's family moved to a new city for her Appa's work. The new flat had no courtyard and no neem tree — only a balcony the size of a rug. Ananya's room felt too small. She missed her old friends, her old street with the corner shop that always gave extra chutney, and the tree that had watched her grow taller every year.

"Nothing here is the same," she told her Paati, her grandmother, on a video call, tears sliding down her cheeks. "I want to go back."

Paati smiled gently on the screen, her silver earrings catching the light. "Come to the courtyard when you visit next month. Bring your drawing book and your patience."

When Ananya returned for holidays, Paati was waiting under the neem tree with two cups of warm milk and a plate of murukku. "Look up," Paati said.

Ananya looked. Some branches were thinner than she remembered. New shoots had grown where old ones had broken in a storm last year. Birds had built a fresh nest, busy with chirps.

"The tree changed," Ananya said slowly.

"Yes. And it is still the same tree. Krishna teaches that bodies and days change like seasons — childhood to growing up, summer to winter. What feels happy today may feel hard tomorrow, and hard things soften again. The wise know: change is the way life breathes."

Paati opened Ananya's old drawing book. Page after page showed the same tree in four seasons — green, gold, grey, bright green again.

Ananya added a new page: the tree in a windstorm, and then calm after. She drew herself beside it in her new school uniform, smaller in the corner but still there, still smiling a little.

Back in the city, she pinned the drawing above her desk. When lonely days came, she touched the paper and remembered: seasons turn. Feelings turn. She was not stuck in one winter forever.

sd2_04.title: The Broken Toy
sd2_04.content:
Kabir's wooden elephant was his favorite toy in the whole world. Appa had carved it from a smooth piece of teak on a rainy weekend, with tiny ears and a trunk that curled just right. Kabir took it everywhere — to breakfast, to the park, even toward the bathroom door until Amma said absolutely not.

One rainy afternoon, Kabir's cousin Leela came to visit with her toy car. They built a fort from pillows and raced their toys across the carpet like a tiny highway. Leela's car bumped hard into the elephant on a sharp turn. Crack. The trunk broke clean off and rolled under the sofa with a small wooden clack.

Kabir stared at the broken toy in his hands. His chest felt like someone had squeezed it tight. "You broke it!" he shouted. Leela's eyes went wide and shiny. She whispered, "Sorry," but Kabir would not look at her. He grabbed the elephant's body and ran to his room, slamming the door harder than he meant.

That evening, Ajji — his grandmother — found him sitting on the floor with glue, tissue, and tears. "It won't be the same," Kabir said. "Nothing good stays."

Ajji sat beside him, slow and steady as the rain on the window. "The trunk broke. That is true. Your sadness is true too. Do not pretend you are not hurt."

She picked up the trunk and the body carefully. "And this is also true: you are still Kabir. Leela is still sorry. Appa's love is still in every carved line on the body. Pleasure and pain visit every person, like sun and rain on the same roof. The wise do not let one broken afternoon steal all truth."

They glued the trunk together with sticky fingers. It was not perfect — a thin line showed where the break had been. Ajji said, "See that line? It tells a story. The elephant fell and was mended with love."

The next day, Kabir showed Leela the mended elephant at breakfast. "You can still play," he said quietly. "Just — careful near the trunk."

Leela nodded so hard her curls bounced. They built a slower, gentler fort.

Kabir learned that day: toys break, days hurt, but the deeper truths — love, kindness, who you are — can stay steady through the storm.

sd2_05.title: The Little Lamp
sd2_05.content:
Diya was six years old, and her best friend in the whole world was a goldfish named Mango. Every morning before school, Diya tapped the glass bowl and whispered, "Good morning, Mango!" Mango would swim in happy circles, his orange tail flashing like a tiny flame in the water.

Diya's Thatha lived in the yellow house next door. He had a small brass diya that he lit every evening in his garden, among the marigolds that smelled sweet and bright. "The flame is small," Thatha would say, "but it is brave. It shines steady even when the wind whispers."

One Tuesday, Diya ran to the fish bowl after breakfast and stopped. Mango was not swimming. He lay very still at the bottom, like a leaf resting on quiet water. Diya's chest felt heavy. Tears rolled down her cheeks before she even knew she was crying.

"Is Mango gone forever?" she asked her Amma, her voice very small.

Amma held Diya close and did not hurry the tears. "Your love for Mango is real," Amma said softly. "It is okay to feel very sad."

That evening, Thatha found Diya sitting on his garden step, staring at the marigolds without seeing them. He sat beside her without speaking at first. Then he brought out the brass diya and lit it with a match. The flame popped alive — small, golden, steady.

"Do you see how the flame dances?" Thatha asked gently.

Diya nodded, sniffling.

"Some people think the soul — the real aliveness inside Mango, inside you, inside me — can be squashed or blown out, like a candle in a big wind. But Krishna teaches Arjuna something wise. The one who thinks the soul can be killed, or that the soul kills — neither knows the truth. The soul is never born, and it never dies."

Diya looked at the flame. "But Mango's body stopped."

"Yes, little one. Bodies start and stop, like waves on a pond. Mango's body was like the diya's wax — it held his light for a while. But the light itself?" Thatha smiled. "The light keeps going."

"Where is Mango now?"

Thatha pointed to the flame, then to Diya's heart. "Where does the flame go when we snuff the wick? It joins the great light. Mango's swimming made you happy. Your happy memories are still here." He placed his warm palm on Diya's chest. "That love did not die. It lives inside you — a light that never goes out."

A butterfly with orange wings floated over the marigolds and landed on the fence, opening and closing its wings like Mango's old tail.

Diya whispered, "Thank you, Mango, for the circles."

That night, Diya drew Mango with a glowing heart and placed the picture beside her bed. She still missed him. Grief did not vanish like magic. But the fear that Mango was completely erased began to soften, like morning light filling a dark room.

Before sleep, Diya looked at the little lamp Thatha had given her — a tiny brass diya on her windowsill. Amma helped her light it. The flame was small and brave. The soul, like the flame, never truly goes out.

sd2_06.title: New Clothes, Same You
sd2_06.micro_theme: The soul is like new clothes on the same you
sd2_06.micro_theme_te: ఆత్మ అదే మీపై కొత్త బట్టల లా
sd2_06.content:
Isha was cleaning the storeroom with Thatha on a dusty Saturday when she found a small trunk in the corner behind old saree bundles. Inside were clothes from long ago — a tiny frock with yellow flowers, soft booties, and a school uniform two sizes too small with a name tag sewn inside.

"Is that you?" Isha asked, holding up the little uniform against her chest.

Thatha laughed, his eyes crinkling like paper folds. "That was me at your age. Same boy. Smaller clothes."

Isha tried the uniform over her shorts, giggling at the mirror. The sleeves stopped at her elbows. "I look silly," she said.

"You look like a growing girl wearing an old shell," Thatha said. He sat on an old chair and pulled at his current white kurta. "This body is like a set of clothes. When I was small, I wore small clothes. Now I wear these. One day, this body will grow old and tired, like a shirt worn thin at the elbows. But the wearer — the real me inside — keeps going, like you keep being you even when your school uniform changes every year."

Isha thought about that, tracing the name tag with her finger. Last year she had been in class one. Now class two. New shoes. A new height mark on the kitchen wall. "So my body changes like outfits?"

"Exactly," Thatha said. "Krishna tells Arjuna: just as a person throws away worn clothes and puts on new ones, the soul wears new bodies. Fire cannot burn the soul. Water cannot drown it. Weapons cannot cut it. The real you is unhurtable — deep inside."

Isha touched her own arm, then her heart. "So when I scrape my knee, it's the clothes — not the real me?"

"The scrape hurts," Thatha said kindly. "Bodies matter. We care for them. But when you feel afraid that one bump means you are broken forever — remember the wearer is whole."

They folded the old uniform gently and placed it back in the trunk like a treasure. Isha drew two figures in her notebook — small Isha in the tiny uniform, tall Isha in today's blue dress — with the same bright star drawn on both chests.

"Same star," she told Thatha.

"Same you," he answered, closing the trunk with a soft click.

sd2_07.title: Win or Lose, Steady Heart
sd2_07.micro_theme: Do your part with a calm heart
sd2_07.content:
Sports day was the loudest day of the year at Arjun's school. Banners flapped in the wind. Drums beat. Parents cheered from the stands like a roaring river that never paused.

Arjun was running in the hundred-metre race. He had trained every morning for two weeks — stretching on the porch, sprinting to the corner tree, drinking water, sleeping early when Amma insisted. His legs felt strong. His mind felt ready, like a coiled spring.

At the starting line, white chalk sharp against the red track, his friend Dev whispered, "If you don't win, everyone will forget you by lunch."

Arjun's stomach tightened into a knot. For a moment, winning felt like the only thing that mattered — more than the run itself, more than the months of practice.

Then Coach Meera clapped her hands once, sharp and clear. "Run your race. Not someone else's. Do your best with a steady heart — win or lose, you are still Arjun."

The whistle blew. Arjun ran. Wind rushed past his ears. His feet found the track. Arms pumped. One runner pulled ahead on the last stretch — a blur in the next lane. Arjun crossed the line second, not first.

His first feeling was a punch of disappointment so heavy he wanted to kick the grass and hide behind the equipment shed. Dev looked away, awkward, as if second place were catching.

Coach Meera brought two cups of water. "How was your effort?" she asked, looking at his face, not the scoreboard.

"I tried everything," Arjun said, breath slowing.

"Then hold your head up. Krishna tells Arjuna on the battlefield: you have a right to action, not to the fruits. Treat victory and defeat the same — both are clouds passing. What stays is the courage to run fully."

Arjun watched the winner receive a ribbon. He clapped. His clap was real, not fake. He felt something steady inside — not happy about losing, but not broken either.

Later, he helped pick up cones and cheered until his voice went hoarse for the relay team. Amma hugged him at the gate, smelling like sunscreen and pride. "I saw you run with your whole heart," she said.

That night, Arjun pinned his race number on the wall — not because he won, but because he had shown up and run true. Win or lose, his heart had stayed on its feet.

sd10_03.title: Goodness All Around
sd10_03.content: One ordinary school day became special for Dev. The story is called "Stars in Many Skills." Dev felt stuck—a small choice felt very big. Friends argued, or a test felt scary, or someone needed help and Dev wanted to walk away. Then Dev remembered what Krishna teaches in the Gita: Goodness All Around. Dev took a deep breath, spoke kindly, and did the right thing even when it was not the easy way. That night, Dev felt proud—not because everyone clapped, but because the heart felt quiet and good.
sd10_03.content_te: ఒక సాధారణ పాఠశాల రోజు Devకి ప్రత్యేకమైనది. కథ పేరు "అనేక నైపుణ్యాలలో నక్షత్రాలు." Dev చిక్కులో పడింది—చిన్న ఎంపిక చాలా పెద్దదిగా అనిపించింది. స్నేహితులు గొడవ పడ్డారు, లేదా పరీక్ష భయంగా ఉంది, లేదా ఎవరికైనా సహాయం కావాలి కానీ Dev దూరంగా వెళ్లాలనుకున్నాడు. అప్పుడు గీతలో కృష్ణుడు బోధించిన చుట్టూ మంచిది గుర్తుకు వచ్చింది. Dev లోతైన శ్వాస తీసుకుని, దయగా మాట్లాడి, సులభమైన మార్గం కాక సరైనది చేశాడు. ఆ రాత్రి గర్వంగా అనిపించింది—ఎవరూ చప్పట్లు కొట్టకపోయినా, హృదయం శాంతంగా మంచిగా అనిపించింది.

sd16_01.title: Growing Good Qualities
sd16_01.content: One ordinary school day became special for Riya. The story is called "The Courage to Tell Truth." Riya felt stuck—a small choice felt very big. Friends argued, or a test felt scary, or someone needed help and Riya wanted to walk away. Then Riya remembered what Krishna teaches in the Gita: Growing Good Qualities. Riya took a deep breath, spoke kindly, and did the right thing even when it was not the easy way. That night, Riya felt proud—not because everyone clapped, but because the heart felt quiet and good.
sd16_01.content_te: ఒక సాధారణ పాఠశాల రోజు Riyaకి ప్రత్యేకమైనది. కథ పేరు "నిజం చెప్పే ధైర్యం." Riya చిక్కులో పడింది—చిన్న ఎంపిక చాలా పెద్దదిగా అనిపించింది. స్నేహితులు గొడవ పడ్డారు, లేదా పరీక్ష భయంగా ఉంది, లేదా ఎవరికైనా సహాయం కావాలి కానీ Riya దూరంగా వెళ్లాలనుకున్నాడు. అప్పుడు గీతలో కృష్ణుడు బోధించిన మంచి గుణాలు పెంపడం గుర్తుకు వచ్చింది. Riya లోతైన శ్వాస తీసుకుని, దయగా మాట్లాడి, సులభమైన మార్గం కాక సరైనది చేశాడు. ఆ రాత్రి గర్వంగా అనిపించింది—ఎవరూ చప్పట్లు కొట్టకపోయినా, హృదయం శాంతంగా మంచిగా అనిపించింది.
sd16_01.moral: Fearlessness, purity, and compassion light up your path.
